historical_timeline.summary: Born Norma Jeane Mortenson in Los Angeles.
Signed with Twentieth Century-Fox as Marilyn Monroe.
Brief admission to the Payne Whitney Clinic, New York.
Died at her Los Angeles home, at 36.

claims.statement: She was born Norma Jeane Mortenson on June 1, 1926, at Los Angeles General Hospital. Her father's identity is unconfirmed; her mother was often confined to asylums, and she spent her childhood in orphanages and foster homes.

source_links.locator: born in Los Angeles in 1926 as Norma Jeane Mortenson; foster homes and an orphanage

claims.statement: She worked as a photographic model, signed with Twentieth Century-Fox in 1946 under the name Marilyn Monroe, starred in films of the 1950s including Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and The Seven Year Itch, and studied at the Actors Studio in the mid-1950s.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her work as an actor anchors the modern social history.

claims.statement: Her mother, Gladys, was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and was institutionalized, for the first time at the state hospital in Norwalk.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history only; the modern episode gives her mother no role.

claims.statement: She is described as one of the most famous people with endometriosis. Her biographer Anthony Summers wrote that the condition was so severe that it destroyed her marriages, her wish for children, her career and ultimately her life; a review of endometriosis for clinicians quotes this account, and museum and medical-history writers list endometriosis among her health problems.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern episode. The diagnosis rests on biographical accounts, which a medical review and other writers repeat; no medical record was fetched.

source_links.locator: physical ailments such as endometriosis and gall bladder disease
health problems included substance abuse, depression, endometriosis and gall bladder disease

claims.statement: The same biographical account holds that, in the days before effective conservative surgery or medical therapy, her endometriosis led to progressively increasing use of strong analgesics, tranquilizers and hypnotics, and to drug dependency.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A biographer's causal reading, quoted in a medical review. It is the reason the modern pain plan avoids opioid and sedative accumulation.

claims.statement: She married the playwright Arthur Miller on June 29, 1956. She had a miscarriage in September 1956, lost an ectopic pregnancy in August 1957, and in all is reported to have had two miscarriages and an ectopic pregnancy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history only. The modern episode gives no role to any real partner.

source_links.locator: two miscarriages and an ectopic pregnancy

claims.statement: In February 1961, after telling a doctor that she had considered suicide, she was admitted to the Payne Whitney Clinic in New York; her stay was brief.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history only, without detail.

claims.statement: The physician and historian Howard Markel writes that she had several mental health problems, including substance abuse, depression and, most likely, bipolar disorder, as well as endometriosis and gall bladder disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective reading; the reason the modern episode screens for depression, anxiety and bipolar symptoms. No psychiatric diagnosis is carried over.

claims.statement: Most of the drugs she misused had been prescribed to her by physicians; they included the barbiturate Nembutal and chloral hydrate.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; the reason the modern pain and sleep plan avoids sedatives.

claims.statement: She died at her Los Angeles home in August 1962, at 36. The cause of death was officially ruled a drug overdose.

source_links.locator: died August 5, 1962; officially ruled a drug overdose
found dead early on August 5, 1962, at 36

claims.statement: A retrospective psychological autopsy based on biographies, films and her writings proposes autism spectrum traits progressing to borderline personality disorder and bipolar disorder; the roster lists borderline personality disorder and depression.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective, speculative reading; not coded and not carried into the modern episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care for a 30-year-old actor with severe painful periods and pelvic pain: a careful history and pelvic examination, suspected endometriosis treated first with an anti-inflammatory and continuous hormonal suppression, diagnosis by transvaginal ultrasound without surgery as the ESHRE 1952 guideline allows, a gynecology consultation on when surgery helps and why repeated ovarian surgery should be avoided, fertility counseling with an ovarian reserve test for a woman who wants children, pelvic floor physical therapy for persistent pain with intercourse, a pain plan that avoids opioid and sedative accumulation, and depression and anxiety care with a structured safety assessment, on the ACOG endometriosis and chronic pelvic pain bulletins, the ESHRE 1952 guideline, the CDC opioid guideline, and the CMID depression monograph.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Monroe returns nine days after her first visit, on the morning of her transvaginal ultrasound, and is seen the same day by Dr. Okoye of gynecology. She started the continuous combined pill and naproxen after the first visit and has had no bleeding yet; she had one day of nausea on the pill, which passed. She has not taken diphenhydramine and has slept a little better with the sleep routine. Her gonorrhea and chlamydia tests and urinalysis from the first visit were negative. She has had her first session with the behavioral health clinician. She asks whether she will need an operation, and whether this will stop her from having children. She has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

assessment_plan.display: Endometriosis with a left ovarian endometrioma
assessment_plan.assessment: Transvaginal ultrasound today shows a 3.4 by 2.9 cm cyst in the left ovary with uniform ground-glass contents and no solid parts or internal blood flow, typical of an endometrioma; the left ovary lies against the back of the uterus; the bowel slides freely behind the uterus and no deep nodule of the bowel, rectovaginal septum or bladder is seen; the uterus is normal in size, without signs of adenomyosis; antral follicles 9 on the right and 6 on the left. With her symptoms and examination this establishes endometriosis without surgery. Dr. Okoye advises continuing medical treatment, keeping surgery in reserve, and avoiding repeated ovarian surgery. Anti-Mullerian hormone 2.6 ng/mL, in the typical range for her age

documentation.chief_complaint: Three-month review on continuous hormonal treatment

hpi.narrative: Ms. Monroe returns three months after her first visit. She has taken the continuous pill daily and has had no periods, only a day or two of light spotting each month. Her worst pelvic pain in the past week was 4 of 10, from 8, she has used naproxen on two or three days a month, and she has missed no work for two months. Pain with deep intercourse persists and makes her tense up beforehand; bowel movements are no longer painful. The urine culture from her bladder infection grew Escherichia coli sensitive to nitrofurantoin, and her HPV, HIV and hepatitis C tests from the preventive visit were negative. She has had eight therapy sessions, sleeps seven hours without any sleep aid, and feels more like herself. She has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

documentation.chief_complaint: Burning on passing urine and needing to go often since yesterday

hpi.narrative: Ms. Monroe called the clinic and was seen the same day. Since yesterday morning she has had burning when she passes urine, needs to go every half hour, feels she has not emptied her bladder, and has a dull ache low in the middle of her pelvis. This pain is different from her usual endometriosis pain: it is low and central, it is tied to passing urine, and it came on suddenly. She has taken the continuous pill every day without a bleed and has not needed naproxen this week. She had one bladder infection years ago. Her mood has been steadier since she started therapy, and she has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

assessment.display: Endometriosis with a left ovarian endometrioma
assessment.assessment: Her symptoms, the examination and a typical endometrioma on ultrasound establish endometriosis. The ESHRE guideline no longer requires laparoscopy for diagnosis when imaging shows an endometrioma or deep disease, so no surgery is needed to confirm it. There is no deep disease of the bowel or bladder. A continuous combined pill with an anti-inflammatory is the right first-line treatment and also covers contraception for the coming year; progestin alone or a GnRH antagonist with add-back would be the next steps if it fails. Surgery does not improve her chances of pregnancy at this stage and removing an endometrioma lowers the ovarian reserve, and each repeat operation lowers it further; surgery is kept for pain that does not respond, a growing cyst, or atypical imaging, and should then be a single, complete excision by an experienced surgeon. Her ovarian reserve is typical for her age. Most women with endometriosis conceive; hormonal treatment does not improve fertility and should be stopped when she wants to conceive. I agree with avoiding opioids and sedatives: pain from endometriosis is long-lasting, and these medicines add risk without treating the cause

recommendations: Continue ethinyl estradiol 0.02 mg with norethindrone acetate 1 mg daily without a pill-free week, and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food on pain days, no more than 10 days a month
No laparoscopy now; repeat transvaginal ultrasound in about four months, then yearly or if symptoms change
If pain is not controlled after three to six months, change to norethindrone acetate alone or a GnRH antagonist with add-back therapy before considering surgery

Keep surgery in reserve for pain that does not respond, a growing cyst, or atypical imaging, as a single complete excision by an experienced surgeon, with counseling that ovarian surgery lowers the ovarian reserve and repeated operations should be avoided
Fertility: a preconception visit with folic acid before she stops the pill; try naturally once she is ready; refer to reproductive endocrinology if not pregnant after six months of trying
Pelvic floor physical therapy if deep pain with intercourse persists once the periods are suppressed
No opioids, benzodiazepines or sleep medicines; heat, regular exercise, and continued cognitive behavioral therapy for mood and sleep

clinical_review.notes: Awaiting clinician review; check the empiric continuous combined pill before diagnosis, the ultrasound diagnosis of a left endometrioma without surgery, expectant management of a 3.4 cm endometrioma in a woman who wants children, the anti-Mullerian hormone counseling, pelvic floor physical therapy, and the pain plan without opioids or sedatives.

provenance_review.notes: PBS American Masters, PBS NewsHour (Markel 2016), Smithsonian Magazine, Biography.com (three articles), Fraser 2008 (open access, quoting Summers 1985), and Dell'Osso 2023 (abstract) logged. Endometriosis is D with certainty probable because it rests on biographical accounts; claims about repeated gynecologic surgery and a contract clause about menstruation could not be verified in a reliable source and were left out.

safe_messaging_review.notes: Mental-health, reproductive and medication claims are marked sensitive and kept short; her 1961 admission and her death are recorded as history only, without detail or speculation; the safety assessment records no ideation, gives lethal-means counseling and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety is reviewed at every visit.
